title: Read the Room: Video Social Reasoning with Mental-Physical Causal Chains
claim: Observable behavior is only the tip of a much larger hidden mental world whose causally linked states must be inferred.
layout: Top video strip over iceberg, downward causal arrows, color-coded depth layers, legend left
description: An iceberg metaphor illustration. The top, labeled 'Visible Physical World', shows four video frames of a soccer-player handshake scene. Cyan ellipses mark social cues such as hands and heads, and A, B and C are labeled. Purple banners under each frame give the social event, for example 'B extends a hand, but A doesn't notice.' Below the waterline, 'Invisible Mental World' fills the large iceberg body. It is shaded in three blue layers for belief, intent and emotion. Quoted thoughts, intent phrases and emotion words sit in those layers. Black curved arrows link events to beliefs, intents and emotions, and link those states to later events. A legend at lower left explains the cue, event, mental-state and causal-chain symbols. The eye goes first to the iceberg and the video frames at the top.
caption: The visible physical world we live in is just the tip of the iceberg compared to the vast, invisible mental world behind it (Zhu et al., 2020). In this example, a brief social interaction reveals complex and dynamic mental activities: B extends his hand to shake with A, but A fails to notice. B then pretends his outstretched hand was meant to touch his head, concealing his embarrassment. C, however, sees through B’s mental state and pats him on the shoulder to offer comfort. In response, B shrugs and gestures self-deprecatingly to ease the awkwardness. Social reasoning is a critical aspect of social intelligence. Yet in long-term, dynamic interactions, capturing subtle cues, recognizing social events, estimating mental states, and identifying causal chains becomes increasingly difficult, making social reasoning even more intricate.
abstract: "Read the room", or the ability to infer others' mental states from subtle social cues, is a hallmark of human social intelligence, but remains a major challenge for current AI systems. Existing social reasoning datasets are limited in complexity, scale, and coverage of mental states, falling short of the rich causal dynamics found in real-life interactions. In this work, we introduce R$^3$-Bench, an evaluation benchmark with fine-grained annotations of belief, intent, desire, emotion, and their causal chains in complex scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce R$^3$-FDT, a large-scale training set generated through a novel automated pipeline with the same chain structure. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art (SOTA) large vision-language models (LVLMs) on R$^3$-Bench, revealing substantial deficiencies in consistent multi-step social reasoning. We also fine-tune a 7B model on R$^3$-FDT, achieving notable improvements across multiple relevant benchmarks. Our contributions are three-fold: (i) a novel benchmark with richly annotated, multi-step causal reasoning data; (ii) systematic evidence that SOTA LVLMs fall far short of human-level reasoning; (iii) a scalable training dataset that significantly enhances social reasoning performance.
